notes.key_messages: Candidates would benefit from reading the question carefully, as it often contains specific information that must be used in the answer. For example, when the question asks for three lines to be drawn, it’s important that only three lines are drawn. Also, the question may ask for a definition rather than a discussion and that indicates the level of detail required in the answer. Command words such as describe, explain, suggest, and compare require different responses from candidates. If a description is required, including a reference to a graph or table, then it will be expected that data will be used in the description given. Many candidates can do this effectively. An explanation requires more than just a description and candidates should be encouraged to practice the difference between explain and describe.
notes.general_comments: Many candidates were well prepared for the exam and had obviously referred to past papers and mark schemes when preparing. This type of preparation allows candidates to express themselves clearly.
notes.1ai: This question was answered well by most candidates. Both leaves D and C are smooth but only D is lobed.
notes.1aii: Many candidates correctly identified the genus as Quercus.
notes.1bi: It is important to read the question carefully, as most candidates gave a definition for genus rather than species.
notes.1bii: Most candidates correctly stated two features of plant cells that are not found in animal cells, with chloroplasts and a cell wall being common correct answers.
notes.2ai: Many candidates correctly identified the cell membrane.
notes.2aii: Most candidates indicated the correct position of chromosomes in the nucleus.
notes.2bi: Some candidates stated where the sex chromosomes are found, rather than stating XY.
notes.2bii: This was a demanding question. Often candidates omitted to split the alleles to form the gametes. Many candidates filled the Punnet square in for two heterozygous parents. These candidates were still awarded marks for giving the correct probability from their cross.
notes.3a: There was some confusion between the roles of different vitamins and iron.
notes.3b: There were some excellent answers describing the selection of desirable features and breeding.
notes.3ci: There were some good descriptions of mutation as genetic change. Some candidates suggested possible results of mutation rather than giving a definition of mutation.
notes.3cii: Many candidates gave radiation as an answer but failed to say that it was ionising radiation.
notes.4a: Almost all candidates constructed a food chain from the information given in the question.
notes.4bi: This question was generally well answered. Some candidates gave names of organisms rather than numbers. Consumer means all organisms in the food web, except the producer. Many candidates gave the number of primary consumers only.
notes.4bii: Candidates showed a clear understanding of the impact of a new predator.
notes.4c: Many candidates gave examples of the organisms that get energy from dead or waste organic material rather than naming the term decomposer.
notes.5ai: Evaporate means to change from liquid to gas (vapour) and the question asked where this happens during transpiration. Many answers stated D, which is where the vapour exits the leaf.
notes.5aii: Most candidates understood that D is the point at which water vapour exits the leaf.
notes.5bi: Some candidates found it difficult to relate the information in the diagram to the structure of a plant. The question asked for a vessel in a plant stem and many correctly stated the xylem.
notes.5bii: Candidates were required to perform a simple calculation, 23÷3 and give the answer to three significant figures. Many candidates tried a more difficult calculation, comparing the rates for the previous three temperatures.
notes.5biii: Many candidates correctly described the increase in rate of transpiration with increased environmental temperature.
notes.5ci: The question asked for the name of the cells where water enters a plant. Many candidates stated a tissue rather than a cell.
notes.6ai: Most candidates correctly identified the valve and muscular wall, but many had ventricle and atrium the wrong way round.
notes.6aii: The pulmonary artery was well known. The question asked for an artery, but some candidates named a vein.
notes.6b: Candidates often did not give an appropriate way of measuring heart activity. Simply stating pulse is insufficient. Counting the pulse in a set time, measuring pulse rate, or using a monitoring machine is a suitable description. Abbreviations for monitoring machines, such as ECG, are also acceptable.
notes.7a: Very well answered. Some candidates did not fully read the breakdown of food box. It stated without chemical change, so that box could not be linked to the small intestine.
notes.7bi: The question asked for mouth to stomach so descriptions of chemical digestion in the stomach or small intestine were not needed. Some candidates gave good descriptions of mechanical digestion in the mouth and the action of amylase.
notes.7bii: Some candidates answered correctly and stated either the pancreas or the stomach.
notes.7ci: Many candidates gave the large intestine instead of the small intestine.
notes.7cii: Most candidates understood the requirement of drinking more water during diarrhoea, but for rehydration it is important to add sugar and salt.
notes.8a: There was some confusion with terminology in this question. Many candidates gave glycogen and glucose instead of glycerol.
notes.8bi: Most candidates selected correct values from the table, and some gave correct answers. There were difficulties finding the correct denominator for the calculation. The correct answer was a very large percentage, so some candidates left off some zeros or tried to recalculate.
notes.8bii: This was a demanding question. Most correct answers described loss of habitat or biodiversity and food chain disruption. Oil palms are large plants so would not cause changes in carbon dioxide or global warming, which were common answers.
notes.9a: Many candidates were awarded full marks for this question.
notes.9bi: Many candidates correctly identified structure B as the pancreas. A common mistake was to identify structure D, the liver.
notes.9bii: This was a demanding question. Candidates understood the need for insulin for regulation but did not specify that it reduces the concentration of blood glucose.
notes.9biii: Many candidates correctly identified structure D, the liver. Some gave C or B.
notes.10a: Few candidates identified all four elements correctly from the list. Many omitted nitrogen.
notes.10bi: Generally well answered with most selecting K at a pH close to neutral.
notes.10bii: Most candidates drew a correct shape for the enzyme activity within the correct pH range.
